job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Threshold and scope.** The definition covers recovery only when a *single vessel* exceeds 10,000 metric tons per year, so operators could stay below the threshold per vessel or divide recovery among vessels. It also leaves unclear how the annual period is measured and whether the threshold applies to each mineral, site, or operator.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear resource coverage.** “Other mineral resources” is undefined and could invite disputes over whether particular seabed materials count. The provision also does not clearly cover processing, transport, or other parts of a mining operation.

3. **Section 2(1)(B)—Discretionary backstop.** Coverage depends on whether the Secretary determines an activity poses comparable ecosystem risks, but the bill sets no deadline, criteria, procedure, or review standard for that determination. Without a determination, risky activities may fall outside the definition.

4. **Section 2(2)—Narrow definition of U.S. person.** It omits U.S. residents, partnerships, trusts, other entities, and corporations organized outside the United States but controlled by U.S. persons. Those actors could argue they are not subject to the worldwide prohibition in section 3(a).

5. **Section 2(3)—Narrow vessel coverage.** The registry applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons equipped for recovery, leaving smaller vessels and other equipment outside it. The bill does not define “equipped,” which could invite disputes about vessel status or retrofitting.

6. **Section 3(a)—No clear prohibition on facilitating or financing.** “Engage in” may not reach financing, contracting, insuring, transporting, processing, or knowingly assisting mining by another party. Those activities could support continued mining while avoiding direct participation.

7. **Section 3(a)—Territorial and jurisdictional gaps.** “Any person in the United States” does not specify whether it covers conduct by foreign persons outside U.S. territory, or conduct aboard U.S.-linked vessels in international waters. The bill does not identify covered locations or provide jurisdictional rules.

8. **Section 3(b)—Broad, open-ended exception.** The exception does not define “mining conducted under” a pre-enactment exploration license, limit the amount or duration of mining, or require the license to remain valid. It could be read to allow commercial extraction under an exploration license indefinitely.

9. **Section 3(c)—Unbounded assessment exception.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” has no limits, oversight, or requirement that activity be noncommercial or use the least damaging methods. A company could characterize extraction as assessment and continue substantial recovery.

10. **Section 4(a)—Registration is incomplete.** The bill requires registration but gives no deadline, required information, update duties, or authority to deny or revoke registration. It also does not require registration of operators, owners, or vessels outside the “covered vessel” definition.

11. **Section 4(b)—Reports may not reveal violations.** Reports describe “recovery activities” but need not disclose location, quantity, mineral type, permits, or associated vessels, and the bill provides no verification, audit, or public-access requirements. There is also no penalty for failing to register or report, or for submitting false or incomplete reports.

12. **Section 5(a)—Penalty limits and procedure.** “Not more than $1,000,000” leaves the amount to discretion without factors or a minimum, and the bill does not specify who assesses the penalty or how it is collected or reviewed. It also does not address continuing violations, repeat offenses, or whether penalties can be imposed per vessel, shipment, or violation.

13. **Section 5(b)—Criminal penalty lacks clarity.** The bill does not define “willfully,” specify whether responsible corporate officers can be held liable, or state how the criminal fine is determined. This could make prosecutions difficult and invite challenges over notice and individual culpability.

14. **Section 5—No enforcement framework.** The bill provides no investigative, inspection, subpoena, or vessel-seizure authority; no explicit agency role; and no citizen-suit or whistleblower provisions. These omissions may make violations difficult to detect and enforce.

15. **Section 6—No enforceable international commitment.** The Secretary need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement, with no requirement to conclude one, report progress, or meet a substantive standard beyond “equivalent” prohibitions. This does not ensure international coverage or address how the agreement would be implemented.

16. **Section 7(a)—Unclear termination mechanism.** It is unclear whether the prohibition ends upon Congress’s finding, upon enactment of a joint resolution, or only after further legislation; the subsection does not expressly say. “Without serious harm” is also undefined, and the bill does not specify the report’s scope or process.

17. **Section 7(b)—Automatic sunset overrides the prohibition.** The Act ceases to have effect after 10 years regardless of whether Congress has found mining safe or an international agreement has been reached. This creates a fixed route for mining to resume.

18. **Sections 3 and 8—Delayed effective date creates a gap.** The prohibition does not begin until 180 days after enactment, allowing activity that would otherwise be prohibited during that period. The bill does not say whether the exceptions or reporting obligations apply during the delay or how pre-effective-date conduct is treated.

19. **Sections 3 and 5—Potentially conflicting timing.** Section 5(a) refers to violations “on or after” enactment, while section 3 does not take effect until 180 days later. The text should make clear that penalties apply only to violations after the prohibition becomes effective.
